text: The S4E lab studies chemically disordered materials, particularly systems in which many elements share a crystal lattice. Configurational entropy can alter phase stability, while the number of possible compositions and atomic configurations makes these materials difficult to search using conventional approaches. Our work develops the computational tools to search that space and applies them to materials for energy conversion and for nuclear environments. Each direction below pairs first-principles calculations and machine learning with synthesis and characterization by collaborators.

directions.title: Hydrogen from water and heat
text: Most hydrogen today comes from natural gas. Producing it from water requires either an electrocatalyst that lowers the cost of the reaction or an oxide that releases oxygen when heated and recovers it from steam, producing hydrogen in the second step. We work on both routes.

On the electrochemical side, we developed a workflow that couples machine learning with first-principles disorder descriptors to screen more than 20,000 alloy compositions for fuel-cell catalysts, identifying lower-cost, platinum-free candidates. With experimental partners we showed that the arrangement of atoms on an alloy surface, at fixed composition and electronic structure, switches methanol oxidation activity on and off.

On the thermochemical side, the group works with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory and Sandia National Laboratories on multi-cation oxides for low-temperature thermochemical water splitting, and a provisional patent covers the resulting catalyst designs. Current work examines which phases contain the exchangeable oxygen, how cation chemistry determines the operating temperature, and how computational predictions compare with synthesis and reactor testing.

directions.title: Materials for nuclear energy: waste forms and extreme environments
text: Fission and fusion both require materials that remain functional under conditions where conventional materials have important limitations. Iodine-129 is long-lived and mobile, and few durable hosts hold it. We showed that iodine substitutes into an oxyfluoride pyrochlore and then screened more than 40,000 multi-cation pyrochlore compositions for higher loading, with many candidates above 33 wt% iodine. That work is part of an ARPA-E program on high-entropy glass-ceramics for waste immobilization and led to a provisional patent on iodine-bearing glass-based waste forms.

Standard density functional theory misplaces the ground states of many iodides. The group therefore builds experiment-grounded thermodynamic corrections and learns them with graph neural networks, so that calibrated energetics extend to compounds no one has measured.

On the fusion side, projects funded by the Seaver Institute and ARPA-E address mirrors for harsh plasma-facing environments and the cesium problem in negative hydrogen ion sources. An Air Force program studies refractory multi-principal-element alloys for extreme temperatures.

directions.title: Data, descriptors, and machine-learned potentials for disordered materials
text: A disordered crystal has no single atomic configuration, so its calculated properties often require averages over many configurations. This makes first-principles calculations substantially more expensive than for ordered materials. We develop databases, descriptors, and machine-learned models to reduce that cost.

Our work includes first-principles databases of high-entropy oxides and their ordered precursors, large-language-model methods for extracting synthesis procedures from the literature, and machine-learned interatomic potentials for oxides, iodides, and alloys. We have shown that structural agreement between machine-learned and DFT-relaxed structures does not necessarily imply agreement in the calculated density of states. Ongoing work examines transferability of these potentials to molecular dynamics and develops descriptors for properties including lattice thermal conductivity and thermal motion.
